accuracy.evidence: Checked against the sources: Lally et al. (2010) report a median of 66 days to reach 95% of each person's automaticity asymptote, range 18 to 254, and that missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation. The lab curve 1 − e^(−t/22) reaches 95% at t = 3τ = 66 days. Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973) found the expected-award group later drew less in free play. SDT's three needs follow Ryan and Deci (2000); procrastination as short-term mood repair follows Sirois and Pychyl (2013).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs young teens actually hold: the 21-day myth (step 3 predict, challenge tag 'days', p3), the all-or-nothing streak where one miss means restart (missed-day toggle, m3, tag 'miss'), willpower as the answer (step 2 predict, tag 'will'), procrastination as laziness or lack of time (step 5 graph, m5, tag 'lazy'), and the idea that more rewards always mean more motivation (overjustification predict, m4, m7, tag 'ext').

lab_distinct.evidence: Six different mechanics in one lab: ordering cue-routine-reward cards for two loops, toggling a guitar and a phone in a bedroom then running a seven-evening energy-versus-effort week, dragging along a habit-strength curve with a missed-day overlay, an inside/outside reason sort, a two-line mood-over-time race, and need meters fed by checkbox changes. No other P&S lab models habit strength over days or friction against energy.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each mechanic makes one claim visible. Wrong card order explains what each loop part is. Moving one item only drops effort to 3, which wins just 2 tired nights, while moving both wins all 7, so friction beats willpower. The missed-day line sits almost on top of the main curve. Delay drops dread then climbs past it. The money and strict-hour cards light no need meter and the strict hour blocks autonomy.

predictions.evidence: Three committed predictions come before the evidence: willpower versus changing the room, 21 days versus about 66, and whether a promised prize makes children draw more or less later. The reveal quotes the learner's own choice back ('You predicted Changing his room: spot on!'), and the step 3 completion message gives the 18–254 range so a correct guess is still nuanced.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions with answer order shifted each round. Every distractor carries a tag with its own explanation: choosing 'Scrolling' as the cue gets 'The routine is what you do', 'Exactly 21 days' gets the 66-day evidence, 'They are lazy' gets the mood-repair explanation, and 'Only competence' names the autonomy and relatedness parts. Verified in the iPhone run: wrong picks showed their tagged reply.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short concrete sentences around everyday cues: phone buzzes, getting home hungry, a guitar under the bed, an essay due in a week. Technical words (intrinsic, autonomy, competence, relatedness) always come with a plain-English gloss. Adult text was simplified to pass the FK target of grade 9.5 or below in validate_lessons.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph carries something the items test: the loop order, friction over willpower, the 66-day median and missed-day finding, the overjustification effect, procrastination as mood repair and the three needs. The family tip is one concrete shared habit with a cue, a calendar and the missed-day rule. There are no motivational slogans or padding.

mobile.evidence: Walked through on iPhone 13: every Show me reached a tick, cards and need tiles are big tap targets, the habit curve can be scrubbed by dragging anywhere across the chart, and every canvas action has a matching button below for one-thumb use. Long captions wrap inside their tiles. Lab file is 19.9 KB, under the 20 KB limit.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action and states the full state in words: cards left and the next slot, room setup with effort and evenings practised, day and percent automatic, which needs are met or not yet. Buttons duplicate every gesture, the challenge uses real buttons with a live status region, and colour is always paired with text such as '✓ met'.

sources: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W. and Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009
Lepper, M. R., Greene, D. and Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 28(1), 129–137
Ryan, R. M. and Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68–78
Sirois, F. and Pychyl, T. (2013). Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 7(2), 115–127
